raw_text:
The objective of this research is to understand the persistent completion-time differences between sites using the same nominal work process. We will identify measurable factors that account for those differences, and find observations that distinguish competing explanations.

Assumptions
We assume that the work processes and the completion times of the sites are distributed normally, and the samples are statistically independent.

Research design
We will use a quasi-experimental design. The sites will be randomly assigned to a control group that continues their work processes as usual and an experimental group that modifies their work processes according to our recommendations. We will then measure their completion times before and after the modification, and compare the results.

Data or evidence needed
We need completion-time data for the before and after measurements of each site. To establish causality, we would also need pre-experiment data to use in a regression analysis, as well as post-experiment data to confirm the lasting effects of the modifications.

Measurement
We will measure completion times using standardized time-tracking software. For the modified work processes, we will track the changes in the processes and record the time spent on each step.

Analysis
We will conduct a regression analysis to determine which factors account for the differences in completion times. Additionally, we will use a variety of statistical methods including ANOVA and t-tests to analyze the data.

Decision / stopping rule
We will stop the study when the results are statistically significant at the p < 0.05 level. Additionally, we will collect enough data to ensure generalizability of our findings.

Limitations
There may be issues with external validity due to the artificial nature of the modified work processes. Additionally, the random assignment may not eliminate all differences between the groups, potentially leading to biased results.
